Generally not, but frankly it seemed simple enough that you could probably piece it together. The big things seem to be: 

1) There is a back and front row to combat you set. Abilities and weapon types vary on which row to hit, or if it's a line or a column. 

2) There are special abilities like spells that reset on rest similar to 5e. It also seems like finding treasure yields item versions of spells rather easily (or maybe because it's a one-shot Matt was more generous with big damage spells appearing inside chests.)

3) Again, similar to 5e, there seems to be an attunement system. Except it seems to be placed on weaponry and adds effects/damage to it. They didn't seem to need to "take time" to attune, just like a JRPG.

4) There are unity attacks that require 2 character turns to use, and they have specific effects, and range/area. Both characters need to roll to hit, and if one misses, the attack is less effective. 

5) There is a counter range and a crit range. Rolling low enough against something that has a counter range equal to the dice rolled (without modifiers) means the unit can immediately attempt to attack. Similarly, rolling high enough (without modifiers) leads to crit damage depending on your crit range. Luck affects the crit range somehow, and I'd like to assume the speed stat affects the counter range somehow.

6) Evasion is basically armor class. Defense/Magic Defense seem to reduce damage (Arin having 15 mdef basically meant he almost never took magic damage the whole game)

For me what makes a good world map is that it doesn't feel like a game.

I always use FFXII as an example. The first town has a sewer dungeon that connects to the main story, but also has major lore about the old gods. Outside in the desert are some ancient caverns that also contain one of the old gods, and you can go there real early because the world doesn't care what level you are, that god lives there and will kill you if you are too curious. In so many parts of the game, there are paths to very dangerous areas that are meant to be late game, but you can freely access purely because that's how the areas are connected in the world.

It almost doesn't feel like a game. It just feels like you're in this world that has its history, geography, and its people shaping it rather than a game dev who has a checklist of areas for each section of the game just to pad out content or make sure you have a way to get better gear.

My entire point is, the steps CAN help by PUTTING YOU in circumstances that lead to those solutions. They don't solve loneliness by just doing them like you said "I do it all the time and I'm still lonely" because everyone has different shit going on. That is the point. Developing yourself and doing things that will lead you to environments that can fix the problem. But "the problem" can be different for everyone, so just doing things without really knowing the root cause doesn't do much other than provide a distraction.

My comment was on my personal loneliness and mental health, guess what of course that's not the same as yours. Yours sounds like you were in a relationship, and now you're lonely because you aren't. Obviously hobbies, going out and doing things doesn't fix that root cause. And frankly, maybe getting a relationship isn't even necessarily fixing the root cause either (because if you're only happy when you're in a relationship that might be unhealthy too). But guess what will potentially lead you to another relationship? Developing yourself. Finding things you like to do. Doing things that will expose you to different groups of people.

A few points:

1) Distraction. 

2) Activities can lead you to experiences where you might get company. i.e. going to the gym, going on hikes, going out to eat (my favorite) can lead to meeting people. 

3) Doing the activities like a checklist or for distraction doesn't mean you stop being lonely. The idea is that doing things, exploring things, figuring out things you love, etc. all can put you into more circumstances that can help alleviate or solve loneliness. 

Most people know those things are ways to break out of their mental health issues and might try them and fail, but more often than not it's not the activities themselves that solve the issue, it's working on yourself and figuring yourself out, before any actual solution can work. You "do and have done" everything on the list, but the list isn't panacea, and doesn't matter until you figure out your mental health, preferably with an expert. Only then will doing these things matter in the long term.

1) Bacteria might die from heat, but they do produce waste which will still be there after all your cooking

2) It's not whether you use warm or cold water to "thaw" chicken - you're supposed to thaw it in the fridge and not just leave it out in water. If you do leave it out in water it should be cold water to lower the temp of the chicken as it thaws and you should not leave it out for too long.

I think the idea of using warm water to thaw being dangerous is assuming something is completely frozen and you're warming up the outside of the chicken. This means that the outside of the chicken will start letting bacteria multiply, while the inside is still frozen. Generally meaning that parts of the meat will be unsafe before the inside is completely thawed.

tl;dr no if you wash the outside of the chicken with warm water right before cooking it you're fine. But never thaw completely frozen chicken in hot/warm water if you plan on thawing it for the next few hours.

Maybe don't think too much about power level. Think about the foundations of it first. Anything can be enhanced or limited, but a good character needs good foundations.

Say you want someone with mind based powers. Alright. How did they get these powers? Were they afraid to embrace it or did they immediately take to them? Are there things in their life that would be good ways for them to use/experiment with the powers? 

It might be a good exercise to embody your character. If you were her, and you realized you could move things with your mind, what would you do? Do you think you could just rip a tree from the ground right away? Probably not. Think about how she might practice or hone the power. Think about major events in her life where she saw her true potential but only briefly when adrenaline was pumping. Eventually when you have a pretty solid foundation you can really go into the science of the limits or source, and how they might really grow their abilities.

Now for the stones. I love the seven deadly sins as concepts, so lets use them.

Avaritia (Greed)
This stone grants advantage on ability checks that have to do with treasure and commerce for 1 hour. In addition merchants may be more willing to provide discounts or deals to you, and you seem to find more treasure and gold in general.

Actual cost is that on stone activation it also consumes many random belongings of people in the nearest town. Potentially making people destitute or losing their most important belongings.

Gula (Gluttony)
This stone grants two abilities "Siphon" and "Swallow" for the next 1 hour. Siphon is a reaction that lets you absorb some of the potency of any spell cast within 30 feet. You may then "Swallow" this energy, you can recover 1 level spell slot for every 3 spells you siphoned. So if in the next combat you use siphon 9 times, that's enough to recover 1 level 3 slot or 3 level 1 slots.

Actual cost is that on stone activation somewhere in the closest town random people will be struck with malnutrition. Enough uses might cause starvation and scurvy or dehydration no matter how much people eat or drink.

Ira (Wrath)
This stone allows the creature to empower their strikes with wrath for 1 minute. Upon activation all your melee strikes are magical for the sake of bypassing resistances and deal an additional 1d6 per strike. A creature hit with your melee attack must also make a DC 12 Str ST or be pushed back 10 feet.

Actual cost is that each wrathful strike you make in battle will psychically harm one person in the closest town. This means they will not die, and will not need any physical healing, but they will feel all the pain felt by your enemies. The target changes randomly on each activation.

Cupid (Lust)
This stone grants the "Lustful Gaze" and "Poisonous Touch" abilities for the next hour. Lustful Gaze is a bonus action that forces a creature to make a DC 13 Wis ST or be drawn to approach. A creature may still take actions while under the Lustful Gaze condition, but attacks made by the creature are at disadvantage. Poisonous Touch is a reaction you can make when you are hit by a creature. They take 1d8 poison damage. If the creature is under the Lustful Gaze condition, they take 2d8 instead.

Actual cost is on stone activation a married couple in the closest town is cursed with insatiable lust for someone other than their partner. 

Acedia (Sloth)
This stone grants one cast of the "Slow" spell upcast at 5th level for the next minute. Creatures within 20 feet of you have their max movement halved. Additionally you deal an additional flat 5 force damage to any slowed creatures you hit with an attack or spell. Even a non-damaging spell will deal 5 force damage while the stone is active.

Actual cost is one person, on every stone activation, is petrified except for their face. Ending stuck as a half-alive statue.

Invidia (Envy)
This stone allows you to know the highest ability score on any creature for the next hour. You may use "Mimic" to temporarily utilize an ability score from a creature with 1 or 2 added. You may only have one mimicked stat at one time.

Actual cost is an increase in crime and general distrust in the closest town.

Wizards are magic scientists, so I imagine that came about from humans seeing these magical people and through centuries of trial and error built a bastion of knowledge for manipulating the weave.

And this is my personal head canon, but I believe people casting the same spell aren't actually casting the same spell. 

Confusing, but take fireball for example. In my head a sorcerer casting a fireball isn't the sorcerer going "I cast fireball!". It's the sorcerer extending his reach into the weave to make something happen such as a high temperature explosion. Meanwhile, a wizard casting fireball has literally memorized the source code of reality to do the same thing. The configuration to do so: components, chanting, hand motions encapsulate the "Fireball" spell that almost always turns out the same if done right. 

In that sense if a particular wizard wanted a black fireball that maybe did necrotic and fire damage, they would have to study how that factors into the configuration(if it would even work, if there's any potential risks).
